title: Capacity and volume
keyIdea: Capacity is how much a container can hold when full. Measure it by counting equal cups that fill it, then record a number with a unit (cups, and litres for larger jugs). Taller does not always mean more; how full right now is not capacity.
familyTip: Fill a jug using the same cup. Count: '1 cup, 2 cups…' Ask: 'Is the tall thin bottle really holding more than the short wide bowl?'

visual.caption: Capacity idea or not? Drag each clue, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: count cups that fill the jug

lab.caption: Flagship lab: fill by counting cups, compare who holds more, record units, separate full-now from capacity, and catch taller=more slips.

kid: Capacity means how much a pot or jug can hold when it is full.
You can measure it by pouring the same cup again and again and counting the cups.
Write the answer with a number and a unit — like 4 cups. Big jugs may be about 1 litre.
A tall thin jug can hold less than a short wide one. How full it is right now is not its capacity.
adult: Year 1 Maths (measurement): measure and begin to record capacity/volume using non-standard units and litres. Distinct from qualitative full/empty language in 'Heavy and light, full and empty'. Words: capacity, volume, cup, litre, holds more, when full.
Common mistakes: equating capacity with how full something looks now; assuming taller always holds more; mixing unequal cups; recording a number with no unit.

In the lab your child fills by cup count, compares capacities, records cups and litres, rejects full-now snapshots, picks short-wide over tall-thin when cups say so, then faces challenge traps for those slips.

choices: count equal cups that fill it
practice.hint: Use the same cup size and pour until the jug is full.
practice.explain: Equal cups poured until full give a fair capacity measure.

practice.prompt: A jug takes {n} cups. A bowl takes {k} cups. How many cups in all to fill both?
practice.hint: Add the jug capacity and the bowl capacity together.

practice.prompt: A jug holds {n} cups. You have poured {k}. How many cups left to fill it?
practice.hint: Subtract the cups you have already poured from the full capacity.

choices: might hold less than a short wide one
practice.hint: Shape matters — count equal cups rather than trusting height alone.
practice.explain: Height alone misleads. Measure with equal cups.

pool.hint: Compare how many equal cups each container takes when full.
pool.explain: Greater capacity means more cups when full.

pool.hint: Write both the number and the unit together, like 4 cups.
pool.explain: Write the number with its unit.

pool.hint: Big bottles and jugs often show litres on the label.
pool.explain: Litres measure capacity for larger amounts — not length.

pool.hint: A half-full snapshot is not how much the jug can hold.
pool.explain: A half-full jug still has the same capacity.

pool.prompt: Jug A holds {n} cups. Jug B holds {k} cups. How many more cups does A hold?
pool.hint: Subtract jug B’s cup count from jug A’s cup count.

pool.prompt: You need {n} cups to fill a pot. How many cups is that?
pool.hint: The capacity in cups is how many you need when it is full.
A tall thin jug can hold less — measure by counting equal cups.
pool.explain: Count equal cups; do not rank by height only.

pool.hint: Every pour must use the same cup size for a fair count.
pool.explain: Same cup size each pour. Mixed cups make the count unfair.
